entry.title: One Hundred Dice Modulo Seven
entry.content:
Problem. One hundred fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that their sum is divisible by $7$?

Answer.

Let $X_1, \dots, X_{100}$ be i.i.d. uniform on ${1, \dots, 6}$ and write $S_n = X_1 + \cdots + X_n$.

Method 1: Symmetry and a one-step recursion

Let $a_n = \mathbb{P}(S_n \equiv 0 mod 7)$.

First, the six nonzero residues are interchangeable. Multiplying by any unit $c \in \mathbb{Z}_7^ imes$ permutes ${1, \dots, 6}$ and therefore leaves the law of each $X_i$ unchanged, hence leaves the law of $S_n$ unchanged. Since $\mathbb{Z}_7^ imes$ acts transitively on the nonzero residues, $\mathbb{P}(S_n \equiv r)$ takes a common value for every $r eq 0$, namely

\[\mathbb{P}(S_n \equiv r) = rac{1 - a_n}{6}, \qquad r ot\equiv 0 .\]

Now condition on the first $n$ dice. If they total $s$, the next die moves the sum to $s+1, \dots, s+6$, which are six distinct residues modulo $7$ and therefore miss exactly one value, namely $s$ itself. So the new total is divisible by $7$ with probability $1/6$ when $s ot\equiv 0$, and with probability $0$ when $s \equiv 0$. Hence

\[a_{n+1} = rac{1 - a_n}{6}.\]

The map has fixed point $1/7$, and subtracting it linearises the recursion,

\[a_{n+1} - rac{1}{7} = rac{1 - a_n}{6} - rac{1}{7} = - rac{1}{6}\left(a_n - rac{1}{7} ight).\]

Since $a_1 = 0$, iterating gives

\[a_n = rac{1}{7}\left(1 + (-1)^n 6^{\,1-n} ight),\]

and at $n = 100$ this is $ rac{1}{7}\left(1 + 6^{-99} ight)$.

Method 2: Roots of unity filter

Let $\omega = e^{2\pi i/7}$. The standard indicator is

\[ rac{1}{7}\sum_{j=0}^{6} \omega^{jm} = egin{cases} 1 & 7 \mid m, \ 0 & ext{otherwise,} \end{cases}\]

so that, using independence,

\[a_n = rac{1}{7}\sum_{j=0}^{6} \mathbb{E}\left[\omega^{j S_n} ight] = rac{1}{7}\sum_{j=0}^{6} \left(\mathbb{E}\left[\omega^{j X} ight] ight)^n .\]

The term $j = 0$ contributes $1$. For $j eq 0$ the exponents $\omega^{j}, \dots, \omega^{6j}$ run over all seven roots of unity except $1$, and those seven sum to zero, so

\[\mathbb{E}\left[\omega^{j X} ight] = rac{1}{6}\sum_{k=1}^{6} \omega^{jk} = rac{0 - 1}{6} = - rac{1}{6}.\]

All six nonzero characters give the same value, and therefore

\[a_n = rac{1}{7}\left(1 + 6\left(- rac{1}{6} ight)^{n} ight) = rac{1}{7}\left(1 + (-1)^n 6^{\,1-n} ight).\]

The character sum vanishing and the faces covering the nonzero residues are the same fact wearing different clothes.

Method 3: Spectrum of the transition matrix

The residue $S_n mod 7$ is a random walk on $\mathbb{Z}_7$ whose step is uniform on the nonzero elements. Its transition matrix is

\[P = rac{J - I}{6},\]

where $J$ is the all-ones matrix. Now $J$ has eigenvalue $7$ on the constant vector and $0$ on its orthogonal complement, so $P$ has eigenvalue $ rac{7-1}{6} = 1$ on constants and $ rac{0-1}{6} = - rac{1}{6}$ on the six-dimensional complement.

Split the initial distribution $\delta_0$ into its uniform part and the rest, $\delta_0 = u + (\delta_0 - u)$ with $u = (1/7, \dots, 1/7)$. The first piece is fixed by $P$ and the second is scaled by $-1/6$ at every step, so

\[\delta_0 P^n = u + \left(- rac{1}{6} ight)^n (\delta_0 - u).\]

Reading off the coordinate at $0$,

\[a_n = rac{1}{7} + \left(- rac{1}{6} ight)^n \left(1 - rac{1}{7} ight) = rac{1}{7}\left(1 + 6\left(- rac{1}{6} ight)^{n} ight).\]
The spectral gap $ -1/6 = 1/6$ is what makes the convergence to uniform so brutally fast.

Method 4: An idempotent in the group algebra

Work in the group algebra of $\mathbb{Z}7$, where convolution of distributions is multiplication. Let $\delta_r$ be the point mass at $r$ and $u = rac{1}{7}\sum{r} \delta_r$ the uniform law. The law of one die is

\[g = rac{1}{6}\sum_{r eq 0} \delta_r = rac{1}{6}\left(7u - \delta_0 ight).\]

The point of $u$ is that it is idempotent, $u^2 = u$, and absorbing, $u \, \delta_r = u$. So in the binomial expansion of $(7u - \delta_0)^n$ every term containing at least one factor $u$ collapses to a multiple of $u$, and

\[ egin{aligned} (7u - \delta_0)^n &= (-1)^n \delta_0 + \left(\sum_{k=1}^{n} inom{n}{k} 7^k (-1)^{n-k} ight) u \ &= (-1)^n \delta_0 + \left((7-1)^n - (-1)^n ight) u \ &= (-1)^n \delta_0 + \left(6^n - (-1)^n ight) u . \end{aligned}\]

The coefficient of $\delta_0$ in $g^n = 6^{-n}(7u - \delta_0)^n$ picks up $1$ from $\delta_0$ and $1/7$ from $u$, giving

\[a_n = rac{1}{6^n}\left((-1)^n + rac{6^n - (-1)^n}{7} ight) = rac{1}{7}\left(1 + (-1)^n 6^{\,1-n} ight)\]

once more.

Sanity checks

All four routes agree on

\[a_n = rac{1}{7}\left(1 + (-1)^n 6^{\,1-n} ight),\]

which is easy to test by hand at the bottom.

$n$ formula direct count
$1$ $0$ a single die is never $\equiv 0$
$2$ $ rac{1}{6}$ only $S = 7$ works, and $\mathbb{P}(S=7) = 6/36$
$3$ $ rac{5}{36}$ $S \in {7, 14}$, each with $15/216$

How small is the correction

At $n = 100$ the deviation from $1/7$ is $ rac{1}{7} 6^{-99}$, and $6^{99} \approx 1.09 imes 10^{77}$, so

\[a_{100} - rac{1}{7} \approx 1.3 imes 10^{-78}.\]

The answer is $1/7$ correct to seventy-seven decimal places. No simulation will ever see the difference, which is the real lesson of the problem. Note also that the sign alternates: a die can never contribute $0$ modulo $7$, so an odd number of dice is very slightly repelled from residue $0$ and an even number very slightly attracted to it.

entry.title: Total Ones in Binary Representations
entry.content:
Problem. Find the total count of 1s when all integers from $1$ to $2^n - 1$ are expressed in binary.

Solution. Let $S(n)$ be the number of 1s in the binary expansions of $0, \dots, 2^n - 1$, each padded with leading zeros to length $n$. Padding creates no 1 and the integer $0$ carries none, so $S(n)$ is the count asked for. The gain is that the $2^n$ padded expansions run over all binary strings of length $n$, each occurring once.

Method 1: Direct calculation

Denote by $T_k$ the number of 1s from $2^k$ to $2^{k+1} - 1$. Then

\[\begin{aligned} T_k &= \sum_{i=0}^k \binom{k}{i}(1 + i) \\ &= \sum_{i=0}^k \binom{k}{i} + \sum_{i=0}^k \binom{k}{i} i \\ &= 2^k + k 2^{k-1}. \end{aligned}\]

So the total count is

\[\begin{aligned} S(n) &= \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} T_k \\ &= \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} 2^k + \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} k 2^{k-1} \\ &= \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} 2^k + \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} k 2^{k-1} \\ &= 2^n - 1 + \left. \left( \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} x^k \right)' \right|_{x=2} \\ &= n 2^{n-1}. \end{aligned}\]

Method 2: Counting column by column

Fix one of the $n$ digit positions. A string carries a 1 there precisely when its remaining $n-1$ positions are filled arbitrarily, which happens for $2^{n-1}$ of the strings. Every position contributes equally, so

\[S(n) = n \cdot 2^{n-1}.\]

Equivalently, if an integer is drawn uniformly from $0$ to $2^n - 1$, its $n$ bits are independent and equal to 1 with probability $1/2$, whence by linearity of expectation

\[S(n) = 2^n \cdot \mathbb{E}\left[\text{number of 1s}\right] = 2^n \cdot \frac{n}{2} = n 2^{n-1}.\]

Method 3: Pairing with the complement

Pair $k$ with $2^n - 1 - k$. Since $2^n - 1$ is the string of $n$ ones, the expansion of $2^n - 1 - k$ is that of $k$ with 0s and 1s exchanged, so

\[\left(\text{1s in } k\right) + \left(\text{1s in } 2^n - 1 - k\right) = n.\]

No integer pairs with itself, since $k = 2^n - 1 - k$ would force $2k = 2^n - 1$ with an even left side and an odd right side. The $2^n$ integers therefore split into $2^{n-1}$ pairs of $n$ ones each, and

\[S(n) = 2^{n-1} \cdot n.\]

Method 4: Recursion on the leading bit

Split the strings of length $n$ by their leading digit. Deleting a leading 0 leaves every string of length $n-1$ once and destroys no 1, while deleting a leading 1 leaves every string of length $n-1$ once and discards $2^{n-1}$ ones in total. Hence

\[\begin{aligned} S(n) &= \underbrace{S(n-1)}_{\text{leading } 0} + \underbrace{S(n-1) + 2^{n-1}}_{\text{leading } 1} \\ &= 2 S(n-1) + 2^{n-1}, \qquad S(0) = 0, \end{aligned}\]

the initial value recording that the only string of length $0$ is the empty one. Dividing by $2^n$ turns the recursion into a statement about the average number of 1s per integer, which grows by $1/2$ with each further digit,

\[\frac{S(n)}{2^n} = \frac{S(n-1)}{2^{n-1}} + \frac{1}{2} = \cdots = \frac{S(0)}{2^0} + \frac{n}{2} = \frac{n}{2},\]

so that $S(n) = n 2^{n-1}$ once more.

entry.title: The Dice Recurrence Problem
entry.content:
Problem: Repeatedly roll a fair die until any face appears for the second time. Calculate the expected number of rolls.

Solution: Let $T$ be the total number of rolls required with

\[T \in \{2, 3, \ldots, 7\}.\]

Instead of the probability mass function, it is easier to compute the tail probability $\mathbb P(T > k)$, which means the first $k$ rolls are all distinct. Thus, for $1 \leq k \leq 6$, we have

\[\mathbb P(T > k) = \prod_{i=1}^{k-1} \frac{6-i}{6}.\]

By definition, $\mathbb P(T > 0) = 1$. We thus have

\[\mathbb E[T] = \sum_{k=0}^{6} \mathbb P(T > k) = 1 + 1 + \frac{5}{6} + \frac{20}{36} + \frac{60}{216} + \frac{120}{1296} + \frac{120}{7776} = \frac{1223}{324}.\]

entry.title: Uniform Sum
entry.content:
Problem. Numbers are drawn uniformly at random from $[0, 1]$ until their sum exceeds $1$. Find the expected value of the last number drawn.

Solution. Let $X_1, X_2, \dots \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1)$ be i.i.d., and for $a \in [0, 1]$, let $T(a) = \inf\{m : \sum_{i=1}^m X_i \geq a\}$. Denote $f(a) = \mathbb{E}[X_{T(a)}]$.

Conditioning on the first draw, $\mathbb{E}[X_{T(a)}] = \mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}[X_{T(a)} \mid X_1]\right]$, where

\[\mathbb{E}[X_{T(a)} \mid X_1] = \begin{cases} X_1 & \text{if } X_1 \geq a, \\ X_{T(a - X_1)} & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}\]

Taking expectations gives

\[f(a) = \int_a^1 x \, dx + \int_0^a f(a - x) dx,\]

with $f(0) = \frac{1}{2}$. Differentiating turns it into an ODE,

\[f'(a) = f(a) - a , \qquad f(0) = \frac{1}{2} ,\]

whose solution is

\[f(a) = a + 1 - \frac{1}{2} e^{a} .\]

Therefore

\[\mathbb{E}[X_{T(1)}] = f(1) = 2 - \frac{e}{2} .\]
